title: Simplified to Traditional Chinese: One-to-Many and Variant Traps
description: A character-by-character s2t/t2s converter makes one fixed choice per glyph. See where variants, regional words, and reverse conversion need proofreading.
content:
How simplified-to-traditional conversion works: match the text character by character against a simplified/traditional mapping table; a hit becomes the fixed traditional character stored in the table, a miss is left untouched. The tool on this site uses chinese-s2t 1.0.0 and runs both directions in the browser, s2t (simplified → traditional) and t2s (traditional → simplified). It has no phrase-level logic and no regional word list, so 「头发」 comes back as 「頭發」 rather than 「頭髮」; the result still has to be proofread against context.

Character-by-character lookup: what the converter actually does

Open the chinese-s2t source and the conversion function is a single loop: take characters one UTF-16 code unit at a time, test whether the code point falls inside the Han range, look the character up in the source string with indexOf, and when it is found take the target character at the same position. The two tables are the S and T strings in lang/zh.js; they are the same length and pair up position by position. There is no tokenizer, no part-of-speech analysis, and no context window, so nothing in the code can weigh a neighbouring character before deciding.

Conversion is a single linear scan, so the work grows with the length of the input. ASCII letters, digits, spaces, and punctuation lie outside the Han range and are stitched back unchanged; Japanese kana and Korean are left alone as well. When all you need is glyph substitution, this behavior is stable and predictable, and it will not corrupt numbers or URLs. The same input always produces the same output, because the only thing that can change a character is its own entry in the table.

import zh from 'chinese-s2t';

console.log(zh.s2t('头发')); // 頭發
console.log(zh.s2t('干燥')); // 幹燥
console.log(zh.s2t('面条')); // 面條
console.log(zh.t2s('頭髮')); // 头髮
console.log(zh.t2s('麵條')); // 麵条

Each of the two mapping strings in the package holds 2,553 characters; after deduplication they contain 2,544 and 2,538. That is the length of the table, not a promise of coverage: any character outside the table is passed through unchanged, and the same holds for any word the table has never seen.

One-to-many: why 发, 干, and 面 cannot be decided by a single character

Simplified and traditional Chinese are not one-to-one. The Unicode Unihan documentation, when it discusses kSimplifiedVariant and kTraditionalVariant, says plainly that conversion is usually character-for-character, but that some cases are one-to-many and need context to choose the right mapping. W3C's Chinese Layout Requirements gives the same example: the simplified 「发」 may correspond to 「發」 or 「髮」, and a traditional character may likewise map back to more than one simplified form. A character table can only pick one fixed answer for each simplified character, and that answer is the same on every page and in every sentence.

Input (simplified)Tool s2tContextually correctWhy
头发頭發頭髮in the hair sense the expected form uses 髮, not the emit variant the table picked
发型發型髮型the same sense again, so the tool once more picks the wrong half of the pair
干燥幹燥乾燥in the dry sense the expected form uses 乾, which the table never produces
干活幹活幹活the doing sense really does use the glyph the tool picked, so this row happens to be right
乾坤乾坤乾坤the table maps this character to itself, so the text passes through with nothing moved
面条面條麵條in the flour sense the expected form uses 麵, which is not in the table at all
皇后皇後皇后a ruler's consort keeps 后, so the 後 form the tool picked is wrong
里面裏面裏面／裡面both written forms are traditional, and which one is used is a matter of regional habit
里程裏程里程the mileage sense is never written with the inside form, so the tool over-converts here
一只一只一隻the measure word is written 隻 in traditional text, which the table does not supply
钟表鐘表鐘錶the table simply has no mapping from the everyday form to the watch variant, so the watch word stays half converted

Read the table once and the pattern is clear: the tool fixes one answer per character — 發 for 发, 幹 for 干 — and leaves the rest alone. This is not a question of a high or low error rate; it is a directional limit. Without context, any single-character table can make only one fixed choice, so the two words above that share the simplified form 发 cannot be told apart, even though a reader would never confuse them.

Variant forms and regional vocabulary: one script, several spellings

Traditional Chinese has internal variants and regional differences of its own. 「裏」 and 「裡」 are two common spellings in the same variant relationship, and regions and publishing houses differ in which one they prefer. The tool maps 「里」 to the first of the two only; the second is absent from the table, so it passes through unchanged. One text can therefore contain both spellings at once, which looks like an incomplete conversion but is really each table failing to cover the other. The same happens with many other variant pairs, and the result is a page that looks half converted although every character in it is a legitimate traditional form.

「臺」 and 「台」 are another easily confused pair. The tool treats 台 as a character that needs no conversion, so place names such as Taichung never pick up the 臺 form, and Taiwan and backstage behave the same way. Both spellings exist in print, but if the target edition requires the 臺 forms, the character table cannot produce them. In the same way, the flour character for noodles is missing from the table: noodles come out with the face character, instant noodles keep it, and conversion never introduces a flour form. A reader sees a word that is perfectly understandable and still not what the house style asks for.

Regional vocabulary is a difference at the word level, not glyph substitution. The tool turns the software word into 軟件, though Taiwan commonly writes 軟體; the mouse and network words behave the same way, each coming out in the mainland-style form rather than the Taiwan one. Every character in these words is converted correctly, but the word itself has not been switched to the target region's term. W3C's Chinese Layout Requirements stresses exactly this: each region has its own normalized forms of Han characters, and in typography regional differences outweigh simplified-versus-traditional differences, so rules should be set by region rather than by script alone. To localize vocabulary, run a regional word list after the glyph conversion, or use a converter with regional profiles, such as OpenCC's s2tw and s2hk configurations. The glyph pass and the word pass are separate jobs, and only the second one knows what a given market actually says.

Traditional to simplified: one-way, missing characters, and lost information

The t2s direction has a more direct problem: the reverse table contains only those traditional characters that were selected in the simplified-to-traditional table. In other words, a traditional spelling that s2t never produces is unknown to t2s, however standard it is. The measured results are:

  • t2s('頭髮') gives 「头髮」, with 髮 passed through unchanged;
  • t2s('麵條') gives 「麵条」, with 麵 passed through unchanged;
  • t2s('隻'), t2s('臺中'), and t2s('裡面') are all returned unchanged;
  • t2s('鐘錶') gives 「钟錶」, with 錶 never turned into 表;
  • t2s('乾燥'), t2s('複製'), and t2s('製造') also stay unchanged.

This is not a wrong conversion but a non-conversion: the output carries traditional and simplified glyphs side by side. For search, deduplication, or text comparison, that half-converted result gives one passage two spellings and makes matching harder, and it is easy to mistake for a proofreading error. The worse case is a many-to-one collapse, and it runs in the opposite direction: what repeats in the T table is the traditional form. 謔 corresponds to both 嚯 and 谑, and 壟 to both 垄 and 垅; t2s uses indexOf and takes only the first hit, so the second simplified candidate is lost for good. Text that was already the standard traditional form, by contrast, survives the round trip unchanged, because that glyph is exactly what the table contains.

So do not treat s2t and t2s as inverse operations. You can check it like this: s2t('头发') gives 頭發, then t2s('頭發') gives the original back, which looks like a clean round trip, yet the correct 頭髮 never appears on the traditional side. Going the other way, t2s('頭髮') gives a half-converted result, and s2t('头髮') only returns 頭髮; 髮 never becomes 发. Neither path produces the correct simplified/traditional pair, so the round trip merely fixes the error in place instead of removing it.

Mixed-script text and Japanese kanji

For Chinese/English mixed text, character-by-character conversion is actually fairly stable. In testing, a string that mixes Chinese with English words, 123 digits, and half-width punctuation keeps all of its letters, digits, spaces, and punctuation; only the Chinese part changes, and full-width punctuation, line breaks, and indentation are unaffected. URLs, email addresses, and code identifiers are left untouched as long as they contain no Han characters. When you process Markdown, logs, or configuration files, the converter does not touch structural characters, which is why mixed text carries the least risk of the cases discussed here.

Japanese kanji are another boundary. Japanese uses forms close to Chinese traditional, such as 漢字 and the word for the Japanese language, alongside shinjitai such as 変. s2t generally leaves them alone, because these forms are mostly absent from the simplified table, but t2s replaces some of them using the Chinese traditional table: t2s('日本語') gives 日本语, t2s('変換') gives 変换, and t2s('勉強') gives 勉强. A result like that is neither Japanese nor standard simplified Chinese; it is two glyph systems mixed together. For Japanese text, use a Japanese old/new font converter rather than a Chinese simplified/traditional converter; OpenCC also states that its lexicon is based on Mandarin vocabulary and does not translate between Japanese and Chinese.

Boundaries and limits: when human proofreading is mandatory

Collecting the phenomena above gives a set of boundaries: when the output can be used directly, and when it must be proofread.

  • One-to-many characters: 发, 干, 面, 后, 里, 只, 系, 志, 制, 复, 准, and 松 each have more than one traditional form, the tool gives every one of them a single fixed answer, and you must correct them by word meaning.
  • Variant forms and regional vocabulary: variant pairs and regional spellings such as 裏／裡 are habit-based choices, while vocabulary differences such as software or mouse differ at the word level. The character table handles neither kind.
  • Information loss in t2s: missing characters in the reverse table produce half-converted output, many-to-one entries collapse to a single simplified character, and the conversion is not reversible.
  • Japanese kanji converted by mistake: t2s rewrites parts of Japanese words with Chinese simplified forms, producing a mixed result that belongs to neither language.
  • Mixed simplified and traditional input: s2t replaces characters only according to the simplified table and does not know which characters were already traditional; a word such as the mileage one, which is also written with the same glyph in traditional text, is changed to the inside form, so old and new spellings can coexist in one output.
  • No phrase-level judgement: without tokenization or context, the tool cannot tell the hair word from the discover word, because both share the same simplified form.
  • Names, places, and classical texts need human proofreading: a surname such as 范 becomes 範, a place name such as Taichung never becomes the platform spelling, the table makes the wrong dry-form choice in classical text, and variant readings depend even more on edition and commentary.

The test can be very practical: if the text is only for reading and one fixed traditional spelling is acceptable, character-level output is usually enough; if it will be published, indexed for search, or involves personal names, place names, brand names, law, or old books, it must be checked item by item. The tool handles the common glyphs inside its tables, while spellings outside the tables and the one-to-many trade-offs remain human decisions.

A reusable conversion and proofreading workflow

Put conversion inside a process instead of treating it as a one-click button, and the results become much more stable. This order suits documents, site copy, and glossaries.

  1. Back up the source text first, and confirm the target region (mainland traditional, Taiwan, or Hong Kong) and the target vocabulary before converting, not after.
  2. Run the simplified/traditional conversion to get a first version; handle one direction at a time and do not run s2t and t2s back and forth inside the same paragraph.
  3. Use the text processing tool to deduplicate by line, sort, and count, clearing duplicate entries and blank lines first so there is less to proofread.
  4. Build a project-specific one-to-many word list (the hair, dry, noodle, and mileage words, plus names and contact terms), replace item by item, and record each decision; a glossary is more reliable than a one-off conversion.
  5. Handle mixed scripts: use the text transform tool to normalize full-width and half-width forms and letter case, so the same term does not appear in two spellings.
  6. When a character is uncertain, use the Unicode converter to check its code point and confirm that the two forms really are different characters rather than a font rendering difference.
  7. Finish with a reverse spot check: convert keywords in the result back with t2s and compare them with the original; mismatches are often one-to-many characters.
CheckQuick actionIf it fails
One-to-many charactersSearch for 发, 干, 面, 后, 里, 只, 系, 志, 制, 复, 准, 松Replace item by item according to word meaning
Regional vocabularyCompare against the target region's common word listChange the word, not just the character
Half-converted residueSearch for 髮, 麵, 隻, 臺Finish the conversion or rewrite the passage
Japanese textCheck whether Japanese shinjitai are presentSwitch to a Japanese conversion tool
Proper namesList personal names, place names, and brand names separatelyConfirm by hand; do not apply a batch rule

If you are only reading a traditional Chinese document for the moment, the tool is enough. If you are producing formal text, treat the table above as a fixed pre-publication check. The converter is responsible for glyphs and proofreading is responsible for meaning; keeping those two jobs separate produces the least rework.

faqs.q: Why does simplified-to-traditional conversion produce 頭發 rather than 頭髮?
faqs.a: Because chinese-s2t looks characters up one at a time, and 发 is fixed to 發 in the table. Nothing supplies the context that would identify the hair sense. Hair, hairstyle, and haircut should use 髮, so add words such as 頭髮, 髮型, and 理髮 to a replacement list and fix them one by one after conversion.

faqs.q: Can this tool distinguish Taiwan and Hong Kong vocabulary?
faqs.a: No. The page exposes only the s2t and t2s directions, with no regional setting: 鼠标 yields 鼠標 and never becomes 滑鼠, and 软件 yields 軟件 rather than 軟體. If you need regional vocabulary, apply the target region word list after conversion, or switch to a converter with s2tw and s2hk profiles.

faqs.q: Why do 髮, 麵, and 隻 survive traditional-to-simplified conversion?
faqs.a: The reverse table contains only the traditional characters chosen by the simplified-to-traditional table, and these characters are not in it. t2s passes unknown characters through unchanged, so 頭髮 becomes 头髮, 麵條 becomes 麵条, and 隻 stays as it is: half traditional, half simplified, which needs manual completion or a converter with broader coverage.

faqs.q: Does s2t followed by t2s restore the original text?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. s2t fixes each one-to-many character to one spelling, and t2s may lack characters, so the round trip closes only for some words. 头发 → 頭發 → 头发 looks restored, but the traditional side never contains the correct 頭髮; 頭髮 → 头髮 does not return to 头发 either. Do not treat the two directions as a lossless inverse pair.

faqs.q: Can the conversion result be published directly?
faqs.a: It works as a first draft, but before publishing you must proofread one-to-many characters, personal and place names, regional vocabulary, and Japanese kanji by hand. If the text will enter a search index or serve as a glossary, work through the checklist in the article item by item and keep a word list of your own.

focus: Confirm the target region and vocabulary first, then choose the conversion direction; one-to-many characters, proper names, and regional words always need a manual pass.
notice: Conversion runs locally in the browser and uploads no text; the result is glyph substitution only, with no phrase-level logic or regional vocabulary, so proofread before publishing.
